title: Beef Tartare
subtitle: Raw hand-cut beef with egg yolk and condiments
excerpt: The French bistro classic: prime beef fillet hand-cut into tiny dice and dressed with capers, shallot, parsley, Dijon mustard, and Worcestershire sauce, mounded on the plate with a raw egg yolk in the centre. Served raw, immediately, and very cold.

recipe.sourceNotes: Steak tartare appears in French culinary records from the early twentieth century, though raw minced meat preparations are found in many cultures worldwide. The French version is associated with bistro cooking and has been a fixture on brasserie menus since at least the 1920s. The name derives from a nineteenth-century French misapprehension that Tatars (Turkic peoples of Central Asia) ate raw meat beneath their saddles; the connection is romantic myth rather than culinary history. The critical technique is hand-cutting rather than mincing: the knife cuts release less liquid and give a better texture than a mincer. The beef must be prime fillet of absolute freshness; only the surface of any piece of meat carries the main risk from bacteria, so hand-cut fillet from a trusted butcher, used the same day, is safe.

content.text: The beef must be from a trusted butcher and used the same day it is bought. Cut it by hand into very fine dice, no larger than 3 mm; a knife gives far better texture than a food processor or mincer. Keep everything very cold while you work. Dress the tartare at the last moment and serve immediately; once the acid from the mustard and lemon starts to denature the proteins, the colour and texture change quickly.

items.preparation: trimmed of sinew; very cold; hand-cut into very fine dice
very finely chopped; optional but traditional
yolks only; very fresh; one per portion

content.text: Keep the diced beef in the fridge until the last possible moment. In a bowl, combine the shallot, capers, anchovies (if using), mustard, Worcestershire sauce, parsley, and olive oil. Season with salt and pepper.
Remove the beef from the fridge. Add it to the bowl and mix quickly until just combined; do not overwork it. Taste and adjust the seasoning immediately.

Divide between two cold plates, shaping each portion into a neat mound using a ring mould or just a large spoon. Make a small well in the top of each and place an egg yolk in it. Serve immediately with toast, cornichons, and additional condiments on the side.
